sections.heading: Standing at the cross and seeing what my sin really is
sections.text: Lord Jesus, I come to you at the cross. I do not want to explain away my sin or make it sound smaller than it is. Help me see it in the light of what you suffered: the thorns pressed into your head, your hands and feet nailed down, your body wounded, your cries as you died. Show me that my sin is not harmless. It is rebellion against a holy God, and it deserved judgment. You became the curse that belonged to sinners like me.
theological_themes: The cross reveals the true seriousness of sin.
Christ willingly bore the curse and judgment sinners deserved.
Honest repentance begins by seeing sin in relation to Christ’s suffering, not merely in relation to personal consequences.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Christ redeemed his people by becoming a curse for them. This directly grounds the prayer’s confession that sin deserved judgment and that Jesus bore what sinners could not bear themselves.
Isaiah presents the Servant as wounded and crushed because of the sins of others. The passage supports the prayer’s movement from Christ’s suffering to the recognition of personal guilt.
John records the crown of thorns and the mocking violence Jesus endured. These concrete details help the prayer look at the cross not as an abstract doctrine but as the visible cost of sin.

sections.heading: Admitting the worth of your blood
sections.text: Your blood is not ordinary blood. You are God the Son who truly became human, and the life you gave is worth more than I can measure. If such a price was needed to rescue me, then my guilt must be deeper than I like to admit. I cannot call sin small when it took your life to cleanse it.
theological_themes: Christ’s saving death has infinite worth because of who he is: the incarnate Son of God.
The costliness of redemption exposes the depth of human guilt.
Forgiveness is not cheap; it is purchased by Christ’s sacrifice.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of the church as obtained by God’s own blood, language that holds together Christ’s true deity and his real human death. This supports the prayer’s confession that the blood shed at the cross has immeasurable worth.
Peter contrasts perishable ransom payments with the precious blood of Christ. This passage grounds the prayer’s emphasis that redemption required a price beyond human calculation.

Hebrews argues that Christ’s self-offering cleanses the conscience in a way animal sacrifices never could. It supports the prayer’s claim that Christ’s blood is uniquely powerful to deal with guilt before God.

sections.heading: Naming the sin that still clings to me
sections.text: Sin is not just a mistake I make once in a while. It is a sickness in me, an enemy, a poison, a chain. It has been with me from the start, and it keeps showing up in my desires, my habits, my motives, my imagination, my words, and my choices. It follows me like a shadow. It mixes itself into even the things I think are clean. I confess that apart from your mercy I am trapped and helpless. I have no claim on the sunlight, the air in my lungs, the ground under my feet, the food that keeps me alive, or the creatures and gifts that serve my needs. Everything I have is mercy.
theological_themes: Sin is pervasive, enslaving, and rooted deeper than outward behavior.
Human beings have no rightful claim on God’s common gifts apart from mercy.
Self-examination before God includes naming sin honestly without excuses.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the painful conflict of indwelling sin and the inability of the flesh to produce righteousness. This supports the prayer’s language of sin as an internal enemy and captivity from which only Christ can deliver.
Jesus teaches that everyone who practices sin is enslaved to sin and that true freedom comes through the Son. This grounds the prayer’s image of sin as a chain and Christ as the only rescuer.
David’s confession recognizes that sin is not merely occasional behavior but bound up with human nature from the beginning. This supports the prayer’s statement that sin has been present from birth.

sections.heading: Receiving mercy and walking low before you
sections.text: And yet, Lord Jesus, you did not turn away from me. Your compassion moved toward me. Your love carried the curse I deserved. Your mercy took the wounds that should have fallen on me. So keep me close to the cross. Wash me in your blood. Make my conscience tender, quick to turn from sin and quick to come back to you. Keep me humble, not pretending I am strong in myself. And let me live with deep joy because, by your grace, I am not only forgiven—I am an heir of salvation, held by you and brought into the hope you have won for me.
theological_themes: Christ’s compassion moves toward guilty sinners in mercy.
Believers are cleansed by Christ’s blood and called to a tender conscience and humble life.
The same cross that humbles the sinner also gives assurance, joy, and the hope of inheritance.

scripture_references.connection: Peter teaches that Christ bore sins in his body so that believers might die to sin and live to righteousness. This supports both the prayer’s substitutionary language and its request for a changed life.

Hebrews connects confidence before God with the blood of Jesus and the cleansing of the conscience. This grounds the prayer’s request to be washed and to live with a conscience made tender before God.
Paul says believers receive the Spirit of adoption and become heirs with Christ. This supports the prayer’s final movement from humiliation over sin to joyful assurance as an heir of salvation.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly reflects penal substitutionary atonement: Christ bearing the curse, wrath, and deserved stripes of sinners. This is historically orthodox in many Protestant traditions but contested in some Christian traditions and modern theological discussions.

The phrase “the blood of incarnate God” requires careful handling. It does not mean the divine nature as such can bleed, but that the person who shed real human blood is the eternal Son of God made flesh.

The prayer’s language about sin being present from birth and pervading the whole person reflects doctrines often called original sin and total depravity. These are central in Puritan and Reformed theology but are expressed differently across Christian traditions.

The original’s question about why creation should continue serving the sinner is intentionally severe. I preserved its force as a confession of unworthiness while avoiding language that would imply God’s ordinary gifts are not real gifts of common grace.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “Before thy cross I kneel” as coming to Christ at the cross, preserving the posture of humility without requiring a literal physical posture.
I kept the concrete images of the crown, nails, wounded body, and dying cries because they are central to the original’s way of making sin visible through Christ’s suffering.

I interpreted “thy love endured my curse” and “thy mercy bore my deserved stripes” as substitutionary language, since the original explicitly connects the believer’s sin with Christ being made a curse and wounded in the sinner’s place.

I translated “walk humbly in the lowest depths of humiliation” as a request to stay close to the cross, remain humble, and not trust personal strength. This preserves the intended lowliness without making humility sound like self-hatred detached from grace.

I rendered “triumphing gloriously as an heir of salvation” as deep joy and assurance in being forgiven and made an heir, so the prayer ends with the original’s confidence rather than only with contrition.
